latin: PRISCÆ illius ignorantiæ temporibus, quæ salutarem Christi adventum præcesserunt, Britannos et Hibernos nostros communem reliquarum gentium sortem subiisse, id est, “fuisse absque Christo, alienos a republica Is raelis, et extraneos quod ad fœdera promissionis attinet, spem non habentes, et sine Deo in mundo:” non est quod quisquam dubitet. “Neque enim Britannia fertilis pro vincia tyrannorum,” inquiebat olim impius Porphyrius, “et Scoticæ gentes omnesque usque ad oceanum per circuitum barbaræ nationes Moysen prophetasque cogno verant.” Neque minus falluntur viri docti, qui Britannos a Druydibus suis in unius Dei cultu semper institutos fuisse tradunt, quam nugatus est Postellus, quum ab He bræis Hibernorum originem conatus est arcessere. Nam et Origenes, quem illi authorem citant, plane contrarium indicat, “terram Britanniæ ante adventum Christi in unius dei religionem” minime consensisse: nominatim vero Andrasten sive Andaten, Victoriæ deam, Dio Cassius, Apollinem et Dianam alii a Britannis coli consuevisse prodiderunt: et de eorum idolomania gentilis ipsorum Gildas tam clarum perhibet testimonium, ut res in quæs tionem vocari non debeat. Sic enim ille: “Igitur omit tens priscos illos communesquc cum omnibus gentibus errores, quibus ante adventum Christi in carne omne hu manum genus obligabatur adstrictum; nec enumerans patriæ portenta ipsa diabolica, pene numero Egyptiaca vincentia, quorum nonnulla lineamentis adhuc deformibus intra vel extra deserta mœnia, solito more rigentia torvis vultibus intuemur: neque nominatim inclamitans montes ipsos, aut colles, vel fluvios, olim exitiales, nunc vero hu manis usibus utiles, quibus divinus honor a cæco tunc po pulo cumulabatur, &c.” Ut de illorum temporum miserrima, et subsequentium felicissima conditione, in epitaphio Nepo tiani B. Hieronymus pronuntiare non dubitaverit. “Ubi tunc totius orbis homines, ab India usque ad Britanniam, a rigida septentrionis plaga usque ad fervores Atlantici oceani tam innumerabiles populi, et tantarum gentium multitudines; Quam variæ linguis, habitu tam vestis et armis?
v0_english: There is no reason for anyone to doubt that, in those times of ancient ignorance which preceded the saving advent of Christ, our Britons and Irish shared the common lot of the rest of the peoples — that is, that they were “without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” For “neither had Britain, that province fertile in tyrants,” as the impious Porphyry once said, “nor the Scottish peoples, nor all the barbarous nations round about as far as the ocean, come to know Moses and the prophets.” And the learned men who maintain that the Britons were always instructed by their Druids in the worship of the one God are no less mistaken than Postellus talked nonsense when, from the He— From the Hebrews he (Postellus) tried to derive the origin of the Irish. For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, plainly indicates the contrary—that "the land of Britain, before the coming of Christ," had by no means assented "to the religion of the one God"; indeed, Dio Cassius records by name that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others record that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons. And concerning their idol-madness Gildas, their own countryman, bears testimony so clear that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: "Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, shared with all peoples, by which the whole human race was held fast bound before the coming of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the very diabolical monstrosities of my homeland, almost surpassing in number those of Egypt, some of which, with their still-misshapen features, within or outside the deserted walls, we behold stiffening in their accustomed fashion with grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once destructive but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, etc."—so that concerning the most wretched condition of those times, and the most happy condition of those that followed, blessed Jerome did not hesitate to declare, in the epitaph of Nepotian: "Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the frozen region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean—peoples so innumerable, and the multitudes of so many nations? How varied in their tongues, in the fashion both of their dress and of their arms?"
v1_english: No one need doubt that, in those times of ancient ignorance which preceded the saving advent of Christ, our Britons and Irish underwent the common lot of the other nations — that is, that they were “without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers as regards the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” For, as the impious Porphyry once said, “neither had Britain, a province fertile in tyrants, nor the Scottish peoples and all the barbarous nations round about as far as the ocean, known Moses and the prophets.” Nor are the learned men who maintain that the Britons were always instructed by their Druids in the worship of one God any less mistaken than Postel was when he trifled in attempting to derive the origin of the Irish from the Hebrews. For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, indicates plainly the contrary — that “the land of Britain, before the advent of Christ, by no means agreed in the religion of one God”; and specifically Dio Cassius has recorded that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons; and concerning their idol-madness their own countryman Gildas furnishes so clear a testimony that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: “Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, common to all the nations, by which the whole human race was bound fast before the advent of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the diabolical monstrosities of my country, almost exceeding in number those of Egypt, some of which we still behold, with their features yet misshapen, within or without the deserted walls, rigid after the usual manner with their grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once deadly but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, &c.” So that the blessed Jerome, in his epitaph of Nepotian, did not hesitate to pronounce upon the most wretched condition of those times and the most happy condition of those that followed: “Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the rigid region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean — peoples so innumerable, and multitudes of nations so great; how varied in their tongues, how varied in the fashion of their dress and their arms?”

latin: Nam quum temporum plenitudo advenisset, “myste rium quod a temporibus seculorum tacitum fuit, factum est manifestum, et per Scripturas propheticas ex imperio æterni Dei ad obedientiam fidei omnibus gentibus decla ratum.” Indeque iis qui in tenebris et umbra mortis erant positi, lumen illud gentibus patefaciendum aﬀulsit: de quo apud prophetam Deus; “Constitui te ut sis lux gentium, ut sis saluti usque ad ﬁnes terræ.” Christo enim apostolis suis imperante, ut profecti in mundum univer sum, prædicarent evangelium omni creaturæ; egressi illi prædicarunt ubique, ita ut nullum locum cœlesti doctrinæ occultum esse sinerent; “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου, non insulas, non continentem, non si quam tertiam habitationem homi nibus natura concessit:” quemadmodum Gregorius Nys senus loquitur. Atque ita completum est quod per Esaiam olim Deus prædixerat: “Mittam ex eis ad gentes in oceano, insulasque remotissimas, quæ non audiverant fa mam meam, neque viderant gloriam meam, ut indicent gloriam meam in gentibus.” Nam “verbum Dei,” Augus tini verba hæc sunt, “non in sola continenti terra præ dicatum est; sed etiam in insulis, quæ constitutæ sunt in medio mari: et ipsæ plenæ Christianis, plenæ sunt ser vis Dei. Non enim separat mare eum, qui fecerat mare.
v0_english: For when the fullness of times had come, "the mystery which was kept silent from the times of the ages was made manifest, and through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command ...of the eternal God, declared to all the nations for the obedience of faith.” And from this, upon those who had been placed in darkness and the shadow of death, that light shone forth which was to be revealed to the nations — concerning which God speaks in the prophet: “I have appointed you to be a light of the nations, that you may be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.” For when Christ commanded his apostles that, going forth into the whole world, they should preach the gospel to every creature, they went out and preached everywhere, so that they allowed no place to remain hidden from the heavenly teaching: “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδʼ εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου [neither the islands, nor the mainland, nor any third dwelling-place that nature had granted to humankind],” as Gregory of Nyssa says. And thus was fulfilled what God had long before foretold through Isaiah: “I will send from among them to the nations in the ocean, and to the most remote islands, which had not heard my fame nor seen my glory, that they may declare my glory among the nations.” For “the word of God” — these are Augustine’s words — “has been preached not on the mainland alone, but also in the islands which are set in the midst of the sea; and these too are full of Christians, full of the servants of God. For the sea does not separate them from him who had made the sea.
v1_english: For when the fullness of time had come, “the mystery which had been kept silent from the times of the ages was made manifest, and through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command of the eternal God, was declared to all peoples for the obedience of faith.” And from this that light, destined to be revealed to the peoples, shone upon those who were set in darkness and the shadow of death: concerning which God speaks through the prophet, “I have appointed you to be a light to the peoples, that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth.” For when Christ commanded his apostles to go out into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature, they went out and preached everywhere, so that they allowed no place to remain hidden from the heavenly doctrine; “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου [neither the islands, nor the mainland, nor any third dwelling-place that nature had granted to humankind],” as Gregory of Nyssa puts it. And thus was fulfilled what God had once foretold through Isaiah: “I will send some of them to the peoples in the ocean, and to the most remote islands, which had not heard my fame nor seen my glory, that they may declare my glory among the peoples.” For “the word of God,” — these are Augustine’s words — “has been preached not on the continental land alone, but also in the islands, which are set in the midst of the sea: and these too are full of Christians, full of the servants of God. For the sea does not separate them from him who had made the sea.”

latin: Et quidem a primo exortu Evangelii suscepisse Britan glaciali frigore rigenti insulæ, et velut longiore terrarum secessu soli visibili non proximæ verus ille non de ﬁrma mento solum temporali, sed de summa etiam cœlorum arce tempora cuncta excedente, universo orbi præfulgi dum sui coruscum ostendens tempore, ut scimus, summo Tiberii Cæsaris (quo absque ullo impedimento ejus propa gabatur religio comminata, senatu nolente, a principe morte delatoribus militum ejusdem) radios suos primum indulget, id est, sua præcepta Christus. Quæ licet ab incolis tepide suscepta sunt; apud quosdam tamen integre, et alios minus, usque ad persecutionem Diocletiani per mansere." Hæc Gildas; ubi quod de tempore summo Tiberii dicit, ex Eusebii chronico exponendum est: in quo ad annum vel ultimum, vel penultimum Tiberii anno tatum est, "Pilato de Christianorum dogmate ad Tibe rium referente, Tiberius retulit ad senatum, ut inter cæ tera sacra reciperetur. Verum quum ex consulto patrum, Christianos eliminari urbe placuisset; Tiberius per edic tum accusatoribus Christianorum comminatus est mortem.
v0_english: And indeed, that Britain received the gospel from the very first rise of the Gospel: to this island, numb with icy cold and, as though lying in a more remote recess of the earth, not near to the visible sun, that true Sun — not from the temporal firmament alone, but also from the highest citadel of the heavens that transcends all times — displaying his resplendent radiance to the whole world, first granted his rays, that is, his precepts, namely Christ, in the closing time, as we know, of Tiberius Caesar (in whose reign his religion was propagated without any hindrance, death having been threatened by the emperor, against the senate’s will, upon the informers against the soldiers of that same faith). And these precepts, though by... were received lukewarmly by the inhabitants; yet among some entirely, and among others less so, they persisted right up to the persecution of Diocletian." So Gildas; and where he speaks of the time toward the close of Tiberius, this must be explained from Eusebius's Chronicle, in which, under either the last or the second-to-last year of Tiberius, it is noted: "When Pilate reported to Tiberius concerning the doctrine of the Christians, Tiberius referred the matter to the senate, that it might be received among the other sacred rites. But when, by a decree of the fathers, it had been resolved that the Christians should be expelled from the city, Tiberius by an edict threatened death to the accusers of the Christians.
v1_english: And indeed, that [Britain] received the Gospel from its very first rising — that to this island stiff with glacial cold and, as though lying in some remoter recess of the lands and not near to the visible sun, that true Sun, shining not from the temporal firmament alone but from the highest citadel of the heavens that surpasses all times, displaying to the whole world the radiant gleam of himself, first granted his rays in time, as we know, at the close of Tiberius Caesar's reign (when his religion was being propagated without any hindrance — the senate unwilling, but the emperor threatening death against the informers who denounced its adherents) — that is, Christ granted his precepts. And although these were received tepidly by the inhabitants, yet among some entirely and among others less so, they remained until the persecution of Diocletian.” So Gildas; and what he here says about the close of Tiberius's reign must be explained from Eusebius's chronicle, in which, at either the last or the next-to-last year of Tiberius, it is noted: “When Pilate had reported to Tiberius concerning the doctrine of the Christians, Tiberius referred the matter to the senate, that it might be received among the other sacred rites. But when, by the deliberation of the fathers, it had been resolved that the Christians be expelled from the city, Tiberius by edict threatened death to the accusers of the Christians.

latin: S. Jᴀᴄᴏʙᴜᴍ Zebedæi filium, fratrem Johannis, abi isse in occidentem, multaque iis locis fecisse miracula; ex Anastasii patriarchæ Antiocheni libro de passionibus mar tyrum, Arabice scripto, quidam referunt. Eundem “His paniæ et occidentalium locorum populis evangelium præ dicavisse, et in occasum mundi lucem prædicationis in fudisse” tradit etiam Isidorus in libro de patribus utrius que Testamenti et eum secutus Freculphus Lexoviensis, “Primum omnium apostolorum prædicavisse in oris occi dentalibus” asserit quoque author chronici, quod Maximi Cæsaraugustani episcopi circumfertur nomine. Britannis, ille qui Flavii Lucii Dextri larvam induit, Hibernis Vin centius Bellovacensis prædicavisse illum affirmat. Sic enim prior in chronico, ad annum Christi XLI. “Rediens Jacobus Gallias invisit, ac Britannias, ac Venetiarum oppida, ubi prædicat; ac Hierosolymam revertitur, de rebus gravissimis consulturus beatam Virginem et Pe trum.” Posterior, in speculo historiali, (in Basileensi etiam concilio, ab Alphonso Garsia de sancta Maria, Cas tellani regis oratore, productus) ita: “Apostolis diversa cosmi climata adeuntibus, nutu Dei Jacobus Hiberniæ oris appulsus, verbum Dei prædicavit intrepidus, ubi sep tem discipulos elegisse fertur: scilicet Torquatum, Secun dum, Indalecium, Tisephontem, Eufrasium, Cecilium, Isichium, quorum collogio lolium extirparet, ac telluri aridæ et diu sterili semina verbi Dei committeret. Cumque dies immineret supremus, Hierosolymam cum eis perrexit, ibique martyrium subiit.”
v0_english: That St. James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, went off into the West and performed many miracles in those regions, some report from the book of Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, "On the Sufferings of the Martyrs"— ...the martyrs, written in Arabic, as some report. Isidore too, in his book on the fathers of both Testaments, records that the same man "preached the gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world"; and Freculph of Lisieux, following him, records the same. The author of the chronicle that circulates under the name of Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, also asserts that he "was the first of all the apostles to preach on the western coasts." That he preached to the Britons is affirmed by the man who assumed the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter, and that he preached to the Irish by Vincent of Beauvais. For the former, in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41, says: "On his return James visited the Gauls, and the Britains, and the towns of the Veneti, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem, to consult the blessed Virgin and Peter on matters of the gravest weight." The latter, in his Speculum Historiale (and cited also at the Council of Basel by Alfonso García de Santa María, envoy of the king of Castile), writes thus: "While the apostles were setting out for the various regions of the world, James, by the will of God, having landed on the coasts of Ireland, fearlessly preached the word of God, where he is said to have chosen seven disciples — namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indaletius, Tisephons, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Hesychius — so that by their fellowship he might root out the tares and entrust the seeds of the word of God to the dry and long-barren earth. And when his last day drew near, he proceeded with them to Jerusalem, and there underwent martyrdom."
v1_english: Some report — from the book on the sufferings of the martyrs by Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, written in Arabic — that St. James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, went away into the west and performed many miracles in those regions. Isidore too, in his book on the fathers of both Testaments, records that the same man "preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world"; and following him, Freculf of Lisieux. The author of the chronicle that circulates under the name of Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, likewise asserts that he "preached on the western shores before all the other apostles." That he preached to the Britons is affirmed by the man who has put on the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter, and that he preached to the Irish by Vincent of Beauvais. For the former says, in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41: "On his return James visited Gaul, and the Britains, and the towns of the Veneti, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem to consult the blessed Virgin and Peter on matters of the gravest importance." The latter, in his "Speculum Historiale" (and cited also at the Council of Basel by Alfonso García de Santa María, ambassador of the king of Castile), writes thus: "While the apostles were going to the various regions of the world, James, by the will of God, having landed on the shores of Ireland, fearlessly preached the word of God, where he is said to have chosen seven disciples: namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indaletius, Tisephon, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Hesychius, that by their fellowship he might root out the tares and commit the seeds of the word of God to the dry and long-barren earth. And when his last day drew near, he went on with them to Jerusalem, and there underwent martyrdom."

latin: Verum Jacobum ab Herode occisum, priusquam apos toli divisi essent in “diversa cosmi climata” (ut cum Turpino loquitur Vincentius) ostendunt alii: et quos ipse Vincentius secutus est authores. Turpinus in vita Caroli Magni, et Calixtus II. in libro de miraculis S. Jacobi apostoli, et translatione corporis ejus (si tamen idem utriusque operis author non fuerit) non in Hibernia, sed in Galæcia ista facta referunt. “ Novem discipulos in Galæcia,” ait in præfatione sua Calixtus, “ dum adhuc vi veret, apostolus elegisse dicitur: quorum septem, aliis duobus in Galæcia prædicandi causa remanentibus, cum eo Hierosolymis perrexerunt, ejusque corpus post passi onem per mare ad Galæciam deportaverunt. De quibus beatus Hieronymus in suo martyrologio sic dixit, ac beato Chromatio scripsit : quod sepulto in Galæcia beati Jacobi corpore, ab apostolis Petro et Paulo infulis episcopalibus apud Romam ordinantur, et ad prædicandum Dei verbum ad Hispanias, adhuc gentili errore implicatas, diriguntur.
v0_english: But others show that James was killed by Herod before the apostles had been divided into the "various regions of the world" (as Vincent, following Turpin, puts it) — indeed, the very authors whom Vincent himself followed. Turpin, in his Life of Charlemagne, and Calixtus II, in his book on the miracles of St James the apostle and on the translation of his body (if indeed the author of both works was not one and the same), report that these things took place not in Ireland, but They report that these things took place in Galicia. "The apostle," says Calixtus in his preface, "is said to have chosen nine disciples in Galicia while he was still living: of these, seven went with him to Jerusalem—the other two remaining behind in Galicia to preach—and after his martyrdom carried his body by sea to Galicia. Concerning these the blessed Jerome spoke thus in his martyrology, and wrote to the blessed Chromatius: that, once the body of the blessed James had been buried in Galicia, they were ordained at Rome with episcopal insignia by the apostles Peter and Paul, and were sent to preach the word of God to Spain, which was still entangled in pagan error.
v1_english: But others show that James was killed by Herod before the apostles were divided into "the various regions of the world" (as Vincent puts it, following Turpin) — namely, the very authors whom Vincent himself followed. Turpin, in the Life of Charlemagne, and Calixtus II, in the book on the miracles of St. James the apostle and the translation of his body (if indeed one and the same person was not the author of both works), report that these things took place not in Ireland but in Galicia. "The apostle," says Calixtus in his preface, "is said to have chosen nine disciples in Galicia while he was still living: seven of whom, the other two remaining in Galicia to preach, went with him to Jerusalem, and after his passion carried his body by sea to Galicia. Of these the blessed Jerome spoke thus in his martyrology, and wrote to the blessed Chromatius: that, once the body of blessed James had been buried in Galicia, they were ordained at Rome by the apostles Peter and Paul with episcopal mitres, and were sent to preach the word of God to the Spains, still entangled in pagan error."

latin: Et ita sane in martyrologio Romano (quod Hieronymi nomine olim editum, supposita quoque ejusdem ad Chro matium et Heliodorum epistola, confirmat Baronius) ut et in Bedæ, Usuardi, Notkeri et Adonis martyrologiis, ad Idus Maii, legimus; “ Romæ hos a sanctis apostolis epis copos ordinatos, et ad prædicandum verbum Dei in His panias directos esse: cumque diversis urbibus evangeli zassent, et innumeras multitudines Christi fidei subjugas sent ;” tandem in dictis Hispaniæ locis quievisse. In ve tere Romanæ Ecclesiæ martyrologio, quod suo præfixit Ado, non aliud de illis dicitur, quam quod “ Romæ ab apostolis ordinati sunt.” In Britannico vero, quod de scribendum curavit Ricemarchus Sulgeni Menevensis episcopi filius, ne nominantur quidem. In apostolorum tamen catalogo, qui epistolæ ad Chromatium et Heliodo rum ibi subjicitur, de Jacobo legitur: “ Hic Hispaniæ, et in occidentalia loca prædicavit: et sub Herode gladio cæsus occubuit.” Addit Ordericus Vitalis Uticensis mo nachus, libro secundo ecclesiasticæ historiæ, septem ipsius discipulos cadaver ejus in Hispaniam detulisse, “ et a rege Galliciæ susceptos, primum fidem et religionem Hiberis prædicavisse.” An pro Hiberis Vincentius alicubi Hibernis exaratum repererit, aliis conjiciendum relinquo : certe hujusmodi aliquo errore dictos Jacobi discipulos ad Hiberniam translatos esse, a vero non est absimile.
v0_english: And indeed we read just so in the Roman martyrology (which Baronius confirms was once published under Jerome's name, together with a spurious letter of the same Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus), as also in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Notker, and Ado, at the Ides of May: that "at Rome these men were ordained bishops by the holy apostles, and sent to preach the word of God into Spain; and when they had evangelized various cities and brought countless multitudes under the faith of Christ," they at last rested in the said places of Spain. In the ancient martyrology of the Roman Church, which Ado prefixed to his own, nothing more is said of them than that "at Rome they were ordained by the apostles." But in the British martyrology, which Ricemarchus, son of Sulgenus bishop of Menevia, saw to the copying of, they are not even named. Yet in the catalogue of the apostles, which is appended to the letter to Chromatius and Heliodo— ...which is appended there, we read concerning James: “He preached in Spain and in the western regions, and fell slain by the sword under Herod.” Orderic Vitalis, the monk of Saint-Évroult (Uticensis), adds, in book two of his Ecclesiastical History, that seven of his disciples carried his body into Spain, “and, received by the king of Galicia, first preached the faith and religion to the Iberians (Hiberis).” Whether Vincent somewhere found “Hibernis” (the Irish) written in place of “Hiberis,” I leave to others to conjecture; certainly it is not far from the truth that, by some error of this kind, the said disciples of James were said to have been brought to Ireland.
v1_english: And so indeed in the Roman Martyrology (which Baronius confirms was once published under Jerome's name, together with a likewise supposititious letter of the same Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus), as also in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Notker, and Ado, at the Ides of May, we read that “these men were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles, and were sent into Spain to preach the word of God; and when they had evangelized in various cities, and had brought countless multitudes under the faith of Christ,” they at last rested in the said places of Spain. In the old martyrology of the Roman Church, which Ado prefixed to his own, nothing else is said of them than that “they were ordained at Rome by the apostles.” But in the British martyrology, which Ricemarchus, son of Sulgenus bishop of Menevia, saw to be transcribed, they are not even named. Yet in the catalogue of the apostles, which is there appended to the letter to Chromatius and Heliodorus, it is recorded of James: “He preached to Spain and to the western regions, and under Herod he fell, slain by the sword.” Orderic Vitalis, the monk of Ouche, adds, in the second book of his Ecclesiastical History, that seven of his disciples carried his body into Spain, “and, being received by the king of Galicia, first preached the faith and religion to the Iberians.” Whether Vincent somewhere found “Hiberni” (the Irish) written in place of “Hiberi” (the Iberians), I leave for others to conjecture; certainly it is not far from the truth that, through some error of this kind, the said disciples of James were transferred to Ireland.

latin: Simonem Petrum, “ duodecim quidem annos esse versatum in oriente, viginti autem et tres annos trans egisse Romæ, et in Britannia, et in civitatibus quæ sunt in occidente,” retulit alicubi Eusebius Pamphili; siqui dem Simeoni Metaphrastæ credimus. Apud quem etiam legimus, Petrum in Britannia “ longo tempore fuisse mo ratum, et multas gentes non nominatas attraxisse ad fidem Christi;” ad extremum vero, cum “ verbo gratiæ multos illuminasset, et ecclesias constituisset, episcopos et pres byteros et diaconos ordinasset, XII. anno Cæsaris Neronis rursus Romam reversam esse.”
v0_english: Eusebius Pamphili reported somewhere that Simon Peter “spent twelve years in the East, but passed twenty-three years at Rome, and in Britain, and in the cities that lie in the West” — at least if I am to believe Simeon Metaphrastes. In him I also read that Peter “remained a long time in Britain, and drew many unnamed peoples to the faith of Christ”; but at the last, when he had “enlightened many with the word of grace, and established churches, and ordained bishops and pres- and presbyters and deacons, he returned again to Rome in the twelfth year of Caesar Nero.”
v1_english: Eusebius Pamphili reports somewhere that Simon Peter “spent twelve years in the East, but passed twenty-three years at Rome, and in Britain, and in the cities which lie in the West”—if indeed Simeon Metaphrastes is to be believed; for in him I also read that Peter “remained a long time in Britain, and drew many unnamed peoples to the faith of Christ,” but at the last, when he had “enlightened many by the word of grace, and established churches, and ordained bishops and presbyters and deacons, in the twelfth year of Caesar Nero returned again to Rome.”

latin: Et Sophronius patriarcha Hierosolymitanus, in sermone de natali apostolorum, Paulum Hispanis et Britannis evangelium prædicasse significat: quod tamen ex aliorum fide refero, mihi enim ipsi auctorem videre nondum con tigit. Vetus quoque interpres sermonis Chrysostomi de Pentecoste, ab Hispaniis “ in ultimas partes” terræ eum cucurrisse innuit. Denique “ tanquam cœlestis quædam volucris orbem habitabilem circumcirca peragrans; tri ginta et quinque annis evangelico pro Christo certamine peracto,” ut scribit Nicephorus, Romæ demum sub Ne rone martyrio cursum consummavit.
v0_english: And Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, in his sermon on the nativity of the apostles, indicates that Paul preached the gospel to the Spaniards and the Britons—which, however, I report on the authority of others this, however, I report on the testimony of others, for I myself have not yet had the opportunity to see the author. The old translator of Chrysostom's sermon on Pentecost likewise intimates that he ran from Spain "into the farthest parts" of the earth. Finally, "like some heavenly bird ranging round about the inhabited world, having completed thirty-five years of gospel warfare for Christ," as Nicephorus writes, he at last consummated the course of his martyrdom at Rome under Nero.
v1_english: And Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, in his sermon on the feast of the apostles, indicates that Paul preached the gospel to the Spaniards and the Britons; this, however, I report on the credit of others, for I have not yet myself managed to see the source. The old translator of Chrysostom's sermon on Pentecost likewise hints that he ran from Spain "to the farthest parts" of the earth. Finally, "like some heavenly bird traversing the whole habitable world round about, his evangelical contest for Christ accomplished over thirty-five years," as Nicephorus writes, he at last completed his course by martyrdom at Rome under Nero.

latin: Aristobulum quoque cujus ipse in epistola ad Romanos meminit, Britannorum episcopum a Paulo ordinatum, in Menæis Græcorum invenio: ubi Aristobuli ad decimum quintum diem Martii, hujusmodi fit commemoratio: “ Οὗ τος ἦν εἷς τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα μαθητῶν, ἠκολούθησε δὲ τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀποστόλῳ Παύλῳ, κηρύττων τὸ εὐαγγέλιον εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰ κουμένην διακονῶν αὐτῷ· ὑφ᾽ οὗ καὶ χειροτονεῖται ἐπίσκοπος εἰς τὴν τῶν Βρετανῶν χώραν, ἀγρίων ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὠμοτάτων· παρ᾽ ὧν ποτὲ μὲν τυπτόμενος, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ κατὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς συρόμενος, πολλοὺς ἔπεισε τῷ Χριστῷ προσελθεῖν· ὅθεν καὶ ἐκκλησίας συστησάμενος, καὶ πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους ἐν αὐτῇ καταστήσας, ἐτελειώθη. E septuaginta discipulis erat hic unus, sequutus est autem S. Paulum, prædicans evan gelium, et ubique terrarum ministrans illi. A quo et epis copus ordinatus est in Britannorum regionem, ferorum et sævissimorum hominum. A quibus aliquando quidem verberibus affectus, aliquando etiam per forum tractus, multis persuasit ut Christo se adjungerent. Unde et ec clesiis constitutis, et presbyteris et diaconis in ea ordinatis, vitam consummavit."
v0_english: Aristobulus too, whom he (Paul) mentions in the Epistle to the Romans, I find recorded in the Greek Menaea as a bishop of the Britons ordained by Paul: where, on the fifteenth day of March, a commemoration of Aristobulus of this kind is made: Οὗτος ἦν εἷς τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα μαθητῶν … ἐτελειώθη [This man was one of the seventy disciples … having established churches and appointed presbyters and deacons in them, he reached the end of his life]. and of most savage men. By them, though he was sometimes beaten with blows and sometimes even dragged through the marketplace, he persuaded many to join themselves to Christ. And so, having established churches and ordained presbyters and deacons in it, he ended his life."
v1_english: I also find, in the Menaia of the Greeks, that Aristobulus — whom he (Paul) himself mentions in his Epistle to the Romans — was ordained by Paul as a bishop of the Britons: for there, on the fifteenth day of March, a commemoration of Aristobulus is made in these terms: “Οὗτος ἦν εἷς τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα μαθητῶν, ἠκολούθησε δὲ τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀποστόλῳ Παύλῳ, κηρύττων τὸ εὐαγγέλιον εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην διακονῶν αὐτῷ· ὑφ᾽ οὗ καὶ χειροτονεῖται ἐπίσκοπος εἰς τὴν τῶν Βρετανῶν χώραν, ἀγρίων ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὠμοτάτων· παρ᾽ ὧν ποτὲ μὲν τυπτόμενος, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ κατὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς συρόμενος, πολλοὺς ἔπεισε τῷ Χριστῷ προσελθεῖν· ὅθεν καὶ ἐκκλησίας συστησάμενος, καὶ πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους ἐν αὐτῇ καταστήσας, ἐτελειώθη [This man was one of the seventy disciples, and he followed the holy apostle Paul, preaching the gospel throughout the whole world and ministering to him; by whom he was also ordained bishop in the region of the Britons, a fierce and most savage people; by them he was at one time beaten, at another even dragged through the marketplace, yet he persuaded many to come to Christ; whence, having established churches and ordained presbyters and deacons in them, he completed his life].”

latin: Patrem vero Lini Herculanum quendam fuisse liber pon tificalis asserit. Nostri Claudiam natione Britannam, et Pudentis uxorem fuisse, ex Martiale poeta colligunt: qui de Claudia ita cecinit: Claudia cœruleis cum sit Ruﬃna Britannis Edita, cur Latiæ pectora plebis habet?
v0_english: But the Liber Pontificalis asserts that the father of Linus was a certain Herculanus. the Pontifical book asserts. Our writers gather from the poet Martial that Claudia was British by nation and the wife of Pudens; for he sang thus of Claudia: "Though Claudia Rufina is sprung from the blue-painted Britons, why does she possess the heart of the Latin people?"
v1_english: The Book of the Pontiffs, however, asserts that the father of Linus was a certain Herculanus. Our own writers gather from the poet Martial that Claudia was British by nationality and the wife of Pudens; for he sang of Claudia thus: Although Claudia Rufina is sprung from the woad-blue Britons, why does she possess the heart of the Latin people?

latin: Quod epigramma cum ad Rufum de Pudente scriptum fuerit: Thomas Dempsterus, homo multæ lectionis, sed nullius plane judicii, ipsi Pudenti nomen etiam Rufi appo suit, ut inde fortasse disceremus, quare uxor illius “Clau dia Romano cognomento assumpto Ruﬁna dicta” fuerit: pari nempe acumine, quo eandem Claudiam “inter ma tronas laude continentiæ clarissimas numerare Plutar chum” idem asserit: cum is Κλαυδίας τῆς παλαιᾶς Clau diæ illius priscæ, Vestalis utique illius nominatissimæ, Quæ contra satis Albulam tumentem Duxit virgineo ratem capillo: Non hujus, quæ eodem cum illo vixit seculo, mentionem faciat. Et quo Pudentem maritum, centurionem aut pri mipilarem in Britannia vel Germania militantem, exulem in Scotiam, ob Christianæ pietatis professionem, extra Ro mani imperii fines, relegatum fuisse colligit, ex illo Marti alis carmine : Cernere Parrhasios dum te juvat, Aule, triones Cominus et Scythici sidera ferre poli.
v0_english: Although this epigram was written to Rufus concerning Pudens, Thomas Dempster — a man of much reading, but plainly of no judgement — attached the name Rufus to Pudens himself as well, so that from this we might perhaps learn why his wife "Claudia, having taken a Roman surname, was called Rufina": with the same acumen, that is, by which this same author asserts that "Plutarch numbers this same Claudia among the matrons most renowned for the praise of continence" — whereas Plutarch makes mention of Κλαυδίας τῆς παλαιᾶς [Claudia of old], that ancient Claudia, that most famous Vestal indeed, "Who against the over-swelling Albula drew the ship with her maiden hair," and not of this one, who lived in the same age as Pudens. ...he makes such mention. And from that poem of Martial he gathers that Pudens the husband — a centurion, or primipilaris, serving in Britain or Germany — was banished as an exile into Scotland, beyond the bounds of the Roman empire, on account of his profession of Christian piety: "While it delights you, Aulus, to gaze close at hand upon the Parrhasian Bears and to bear the stars of the Scythian pole."
v1_english: Although this epigram was written to Rufus about Pudens, Thomas Dempster — a man of much reading but plainly of no judgement — even assigned the name Rufus to Pudens himself, so that from this we might perhaps learn why his wife "Claudia, having taken on the Roman cognomen, was called Rufina": with that same acumen, indeed, by which he likewise asserts that "Plutarch numbers this same Claudia among the matrons most renowned for the praise of continence" — although Plutarch makes mention of Κλαυδίας τῆς παλαιᾶς [that ancient Claudia], that most celebrated Vestal, of course, "Who, against the swelling Albula, well enough / Drew the vessel with her maiden's hair," and not of this Claudia, who lived in the same age as Pudens. And [it is with the like acumen] that he gathers, from that poem of Martial, that the husband Pudens, a centurion or primipilus serving in Britain or Germany, was banished as an exile into Scotland, beyond the bounds of the Roman empire, on account of his profession of Christian piety: "While it delights you, Aulus, to behold the Parrhasian / oxen at close range, and to bear the stars of the Scythian pole."

latin: Ubi argutissimus criticus Scotici vocabulum, pro Scythici, reponendum esse conjicit: oblitus, apud Claudianum, Apollinarem Sidonium ac veteres illos, primam Scotici nominis syllabam semper productam legi; et in antiquis manuscriptis Scottos geminata litera passim exarari con suevisse. Neque sui dissimilis est, quum addit, Perso nium “probare in conversione Anglicana Claudiam non potuisse esse Anglam,” quasi quisquam eam Dempsteri insaniret insaniam, ut Claudiæ temporibus Angliam quæ reret in Britannia: aut id argumentatione sua conficere non conaretur Personius, B. Claudiam cujus Paulus meminit, non fuisse Britannam illam, cujus formæ decus Trajano imperante Martialis laudaverit; et consequenter, absque ullo fundamento vel Scotam constitui vel Anglam. Quan quam argumentum illud, quo potissimum ille nititur, a temporis ratione deductum, non multum urgeat. Neque enim si in undecimo quem citavimus epigrammatum libello occurrrunt aliqua sub tertio vel Nervæ vel Trajani consu latu conscripta carmina; sequetur, et reliqua omnia eodem tempore fuisse composita. Et licet sub Trajano mortem poeta obierit: senem tamen decessisse cogitandum est, et prius familiariter usum esse Silio Italico, secundi belli Punici scriptore: quo consulatum gerente, Neronem in teriisse, et alii authores confirmant, et ipse Martialis signi ficat illis de Silio versiculis : Postquam bis senis ingentem fascibus annum Rexerat, asserto qui sacer orbe fuit : Emeritos Musis et Phœbo tradidit annos, Proque suo celebrat nunc Helicona foro.
v0_english: Here that most ingenious critic conjectures that the word Scotici ought to be substituted for Scythici — forgetting that in Claudian, Sidonius Apollinaris, and those ancient writers, the first syllable of the name Scotici is always read as long, and that in old manuscripts Scotti was commonly everywhere written with a doubled letter. Nor is he unlike himself when he adds that Persons "proves, in his treatise on the English conversion, that Claudia could not have been English" — as though anyone would rave with Dempster's madness so far as to look for England in Britain in Claudia's day, or as though Persons were not striving to establish by his argument that the blessed Claudia whom Paul mentions was not that British woman whose beauty Martial praised under the reign of Trajan, and that consequently she is set up, without any foundation, as either a Scot or an Englishwoman. And yet that argument on which he chiefly relies, drawn from the reckoning of dates, carries little force; for even if in the eleventh book of epigrams which I cited there occur some poems written under the third consulship of either Nerva or Trajan, it does not follow that all the rest were composed at the same time. And although the poet died under Trajan, one must nevertheless suppose that he passed away an old man, and that he had earlier been on familiar terms with Silius Italicus, the writer of the Second Punic War. the author of the Punica; and that Nero perished during his consulship is confirmed both by other authorities and by Martial himself, who indicates as much in those verses about Silius: After he had governed the mighty year with its twice-six fasces — he who was hallowed when the world had been set free — he devoted his remaining years to the Muses and to Phoebus, and now frequents Helicon in place of his own forum.
v1_english: Here the most ingenious critic conjectures that the word "Scotici" should be substituted for "Scythici" — forgetting that in Claudian, Apollinaris Sidonius, and those ancient writers the first syllable of the name "Scoti" is always read long, and that in old manuscripts "Scotti" was regularly written throughout with a doubled letter. And he is quite in character when he adds that Persons "proves, in his "Conversion of England," that Claudia could not have been an Englishwoman" — as though anyone would rave with Dempster's madness and search for England in Britain in Claudia's day, or as though Persons were not trying to establish by his argument that the blessed Claudia whom Paul mentions was not that British woman whose beauty Martial praised under the emperor Trajan, and was consequently set up, without any foundation, as either a Scotswoman or an Englishwoman. And yet that argument on which he chiefly relies, drawn from chronological reckoning, carries little weight. For even if, in the eleventh book of epigrams which I cited, there occur certain poems composed under the third consulship of either Nerva or Trajan, it does not follow that all the rest were composed at the same time. And although the poet died under Trajan, it must be supposed that he died an old man, and that he had earlier been on familiar terms with Silius Italicus, the writer on the Second Punic War — during whose consulship Nero perished, as both other authorities confirm and Martial himself indicates in those verses about Silius: "After he had governed the mighty year with its twice-six fasces — he who was hallowed when the world had been set free — he gave his retirement years to the Muses and to Phoebus, and now frequents Helicon in place of his own forum."
